TITLE: Concurrent Management of an Exotic Species and Initial Restoration Efforts in Forests
SPECIES: T1=Sanguinaria canadensis (S. canadensis); T2=Alliaria petiolata (A. petiolata)
CONTEXT: Although the long-term challenge in solving the impacts of exotic species is to halt fragmentation on local and landscape scales, the immediate challenge is that remnant forests must be protected and restored before too many species are extirpated. One approach is to simultaneously manage exotic invaders and restore species; care must be taken because exotic removal is not always the best course of action in general, and it may just create opportunities for other exotic species. It may be useful to reintroduce native species that compete successfully with exotics as a useful, albeit small, first step to restoring forest ecosystems. The site chosen was a degraded woodlot (total area = 31,916 m2) located on a farm approximately 16 km northwest of Waterloo, Ontario, Canada. Experiments were conducted on the first 50 m the woodlot near the identifiable edge of the northern face. The choice of experimental locations within the site was based on the criteria that they had large populations of Alliaria petiolata but few or no individuals of Sanguinaria canadensis. There were few other species present at any time of the year in the plots; hence, there was no need to remove them. The collective background density was a maximum of 4 plants/ m2 of some or all of Common spring beauty (Claytonia virginica L.), Yellow trout lily (Erythronium americanum Ker.), Dame's rocket (Hesperis matronalis L.), Canada avens (Geum canadense L.), Herb-robert (Geranium robertianum L.), Canada bluegrass or wiregrass (Poa compressa L.), and Woodland speargrass (Poa nemoralis L.). There were no other shrubs, saplings, or mature trees rooted in any of the plots. Because competitive effects often become nonlinear at extremely low densities, more emphasis was placed on densities below this mean and standard error.
TEXT:
[1] (abs) One of the proximate results of forest fragmentation, and a cause of continued microenvironmental change and exacerbation of ecological problems, is increased invasions by weedy plant species.
[2] (abs) One such example is Alliaria petiolata (Brassicaceae), a serious pest threatening much of eastern North America.
[3] (abs) Alliaria petiolata impedes mitigation of fragmentation and restoration efforts because it tends to outcompete and possibly extirpate much of the native understory species on localized scales.
[4] (abs) As part of a strategy to address the problems of fragmented habitats, an experiment was conducted to determine whether Sanguinaria canadensis (Papaveraceae) could outcompete A. petiolata.
[5] (abs) Using an additive design, I transplanted S. canadensis at densities of 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, and 20 ramets/m2 in 1997 and allowed them to interact with initial A. petiolata densities of 128 seedlings and 31 rosettes/m2.
[6] (abs) As of 2000, multivariate analyses of variance with repeated measures and simple analyses of variance indicated that initial S. canadensis densities of as little as 5 ramets/m2 suppressed A. petiolata.
[7] (abs) Initial S. canadensis densities of 9 and 11 ramets/m2 resulted in the lowest numbers of late-spring seedlings, numbers and sizes of year 1 and 2 rosettes, numbers and gross areas of stem leaves, numbers of flowering individuals, number of flowers, number of fruits (siliques), and height at flowering.
[8] (abs) While it remains to be tested whether this will continue and if the reestablishment of S. canadensis will help reassemble forest ecosystems, the experiments indicated that transplanting S. canadensis was effective at mitigating the spread of A. petiolata.
[9] (res) The results for the competition experiments generally showed that the initial densities of S. canadensis had different effects on A. petiolata in subsequent years.
[10] (res) The significant time $\times$ density interactions indicated that the effects of initial densities changed over time as the populations of A. petiolata were affected by competition with S. canadensis after the first season.
[11] (res) The only variables not affected were number of seedlings in early spring, number of seedlings in autumn, change in numbers of seedlings from autumn to spring, change in number of year 2 rosettes from early to late spring.
[12] (res) These were analyzed only in the unreported initial analyses and are excluded from Table 1.
[13] (res) Generally, initial S. canadensis densities of 7, 9, and 11 ramets/m2 suppressed A. petiolata most.
[14] (res) When within-year ANOVAs were run for the 2000 data, there were no significant differences on most variables measured for A. petiolata among initial S. canadensis densities of 9, 11, 15, and 20 ramets/m2, though 9 and 11 ramets/m2 tended to be the most effective, e.g., see the response of the numbers of seedlings in late spring and leaf area in Tables 1–3.
[15] (res) At lower initial densities (3 ramets/m2 or less), S. canadensis usually could not compete with A. petiolata.
[16] (res) At the two highest initial densities (15 and 20 ramets/m2), S. canadensis ultimately declined, probably through density-dependent intraspecific competition, and more seedlings and rosettes of A. petiolata survived to compete with S. canadensis.
[17] (res) By 2000, this meant that the higher densities of S. canadensis provided no additional benefit in suppressing A. petiolata and fared slightly, but not significantly, worse than densities of 5, 7, 9, and 11 ramets/m2.
[18] (res) The increase in the number of leaves of S. canadensis at initial intermediate densities of 9 and 11 ramets/m2 to levels equal to or near the highest initial density of 20 ramets/m2 indicates that these intermediate densities were most useful in competing with A. petiolata.
[19] (res) However, I do not suggest that this one measure is a substitute for a complete response surface test for intra- and interspecific competition affecting S. canadensis.
[20] (res) Early-spring emergence of seedlings in A. petiolata remained relatively constant, probably indicating that an existing, extensive seed bank persisted throughout and was not affected after only 4 years.
[21] (res) This was not surprising because soil cores of seven woodlots of similar area and within 5 km of my study site have revealed that the mean number of seeds of A. petiolata was 2,567 ($\pm 478$) per m3.
[22] (res) Additionally, S. canadensis probably leafs too late to suppress most seed germination and seedling emergence in A. petiolata.
[23] (res) By the time the first leaves of S. canadensis appeared, most of the seedlings of A. petiolata have emerged and leafed.
[24] (res) However, leafing at (initial) densities of S. canadensis above 7 ramets/m2 was early enough to kill significantly more seedlings of A. petiolata before they matured; both the numbers of late-spring seedlings and the change in numbers of seedlings between early and late spring declined significantly at these densities by 2000.
[25] (res) By summer, however, the leaves of S. canadensis senesced and, with such a large seed bank, there were no differences between density treatments in the numbers of autumn seedlings that emerged during summer or change in numbers of seedlings of A. petiolata between late spring and autumn.
[26] (res) The numbers and sizes of rosettes of A. petiolata were affected more seriously in the sense that, by 2000, the initial densities of even 5 ramets/m2 of S. canadensis significantly harmed early-spring, late-spring, and autumn rosettes.
[27] (res) Below this density, rosette numbers and sizes increased over time.
[28] (res) Because there were no significant changes in the numbers of rosettes between year 1 autumn and year 2 early spring or year 2 early spring and year 2 late spring, it means that the impact was probably related to the effect of S. canadensis on seedlings as opposed to any direct suppression of rosettes of A. petiolata.
[29] (res) Higher densities of S. canadensis likely killed or harmed enough seedlings of A. petiolata so that there were fewer survivors to produce year 1 rosettes, and those that survived produced smaller rosettes.
[30] (res) The autumn data included later emerging A. petiolata that escaped competition from S. canadensis, but any later emergents were not great in numbers.
[31] (res) Although I have not reported these in detail, a maximum of 4.2% year 1 rosettes and seedlings came from individuals that emerged after mid-June in any year.

TITLE: Concurrent Management of an Exotic Species and Initial Restoration Efforts in Forests
SPECIES: T1=Sanguinaria canadensis (S. canadensis); T2=Alliaria petiolata (A. petiolata)
CONTEXT: Although the long-term challenge in solving the impacts of exotic species is to halt fragmentation on local and landscape scales, the immediate challenge is that remnant forests must be protected and restored before too many species are extirpated. One approach is to simultaneously manage exotic invaders and restore species; care must be taken because exotic removal is not always the best course of action in general, and it may just create opportunities for other exotic species. It may be useful to reintroduce native species that compete successfully with exotics as a useful, albeit small, first step to restoring forest ecosystems. The site chosen was a degraded woodlot (total area = 31,916 m2) located on a farm approximately 16 km northwest of Waterloo, Ontario, Canada. Experiments were conducted on the first 50 m the woodlot near the identifiable edge of the northern face. The choice of experimental locations within the site was based on the criteria that they had large populations of Alliaria petiolata but few or no individuals of Sanguinaria canadensis. There were few other species present at any time of the year in the plots; hence, there was no need to remove them. The collective background density was a maximum of 4 plants/ m2 of some or all of Common spring beauty (Claytonia virginica L.), Yellow trout lily (Erythronium americanum Ker.), Dame's rocket (Hesperis matronalis L.), Canada avens (Geum canadense L.), Herb-robert (Geranium robertianum L.), Canada bluegrass or wiregrass (Poa compressa L.), and Woodland speargrass (Poa nemoralis L.). There were no other shrubs, saplings, or mature trees rooted in any of the plots. Because competitive effects often become nonlinear at extremely low densities, more emphasis was placed on densities below this mean and standard error.
TEXT:
[32] (res) Tests were based on data collected from 40 plots observed during the first week of April through the last week of September from 1997 to 2000.
[33] (res) Results are reported only for the combined MANOVAR using variables reported as significant in constrained MANOVARs (see text).
[34] (res) For density of S. canadensis (the between-subjects effect), data are reported as the standard used for repeated-measured ANOVA (MS, F, p).
[35] (res) For time and time $\times$ density (within-subjects effects), data are reported using F, p, and Pillai's Trace because the latter is the actual test for significant differences of the repeated factor of time (and time $\times$ density) within subjects.
[36] (res) MS=mean square error.
[37] (res) The number of stem leaves, gross leaf area, number of flowers, number of siliques, and height at final flowering were all significantly suppressed by S. canadensis at intermediate and higher densities of 7, 9, 11, 15, and 20 ramets/m2.
[38] (res) These are all good indicators that density-dependent competition from S. canadensis had a significant effect on A. petiolata.
[39] (res) It appears that intermediate and higher densities of S. canadensis deprived A. petiolata of sufficient resources to produce large leaves, flowers, and fruits, indicating that both vegetative and reproductive allocations were affected.
[40] (res) The inability of A. petiolata to allocate more resources to grow taller under intermediate and higher densities of S. canadensis means that it either had insufficient resources or could not reallocate resources quickly enough when in competition.
[41] (dis) For ecological restoration, the results suggest that planting intermediate densities of Sanguinaria canadensis is a good strategy in managing invasions by Alliaria petiolata.
[42] (dis) Although the lack of an effect on early- and late-season numbers of seedlings might seem to indicate that the situation is hopeless, this is true only if the goal is to quickly reduce short-term populations of A. petiolata.
[43] (dis) This was not the purpose here.
[44] (dis) Even though the spring populations of A. petiolata remained high, they did not worsen when densities of five or more ramets per square meter of S. canadensis were transplanted.
[45] (dis) Given the reduced fruit set, a long-term implication is that populations of A. petiolata will decrease locally as long as immigration of new seeds does not counter this.
[46] (dis) In a small woodlot, this is likely to occur with restoration efforts.
[47] (dis) In larger, contiguous woodland infested with A. petiolata, this would be more difficult (e.g., Drayton & Primack 1999; Nuzzo 1999).
[48] (dis) All else being equal, densities of 9 and 11 ramets/m2 of S. canadensis resulted in more successful competition with A. petiolata.
[49] (dis) But for what resources was there competition?
[50] (dis) I did not design the experiment to test directly for the mechanism of competition, but the literature offers strong ideas.
[51] (dis) Although competition can be for any limited resource, most understory plants tend to compete for light because nutrients and water are normally plentiful.
[52] (dis) Previous evidence for competitive superiority of A. petiolata indicates that its early emergence and competition for light are most important.
[53] (dis) Ultimately, a more complicated competition experiment will be useful in elucidating mechanisms, that is, test for the complexities of different resources, environmental heterogeneity, size- and density-dependent competition, genotype by environment interactions.
[54] (dis) However, the scope of my experiment already was labor intensive and complex; hence, this hypothetical experiment may be too unwieldy.
[55] (dis) My study has determined that some densities of S. canadensis were indeed successful at halting the dominance of A. petiolata in early to late spring, and S. canadensis established itself to begin ecological restoration.
[56] (dis) This success may provide opportunity for other native species to reestablish from nearby propagules sources and increase the impact of ecological restoration, but thus remains to be tested explicitly.
[57] (dis) In my study, there is no evidence yet of regeneration of other native species from the existing propagules.
[58] (dis) By 2000, I had not detected any increase in other native species or other exotics in any treatments; the data were not reported because of the lack of any large numbers of individuals and the subsequent lack of any trends.
[59] (dis) The absence of any significant reestablishment of other natives may be explained by their inability to compete with the still high densities of A. petiolata, the generally higher densities of S. canadensis, a lack of seed bank or immigration sources, and an ecosystem that cannot support their natural regeneration, especially in terms of the mycorrhizal and decomposition communities.
[60] (dis) Of course, it may be a simple case if being too early in ecological restoration to expect and detect any changes for species other than the transplanted S. canadensis.
[61] (dis) Tests were based on data collected from 40 plots observed during the first week of April through the last week of September from 1997 to 2000.
[62] (dis) Within each row, data followed by the same letter are not significantly different according to Tukey's test for HSD0.05. effective on a local scale of a couple of hundred meters at most.
[63] (dis) Ramets of S. canadensis may be rescued from nearby development, grown locally from a ramet or seed stock, or purchased locally for approximately US \$2.00 per 8-cm pot.
[64] (dis) The transplanting in my study required about 8 hours for 40 m2 of plots, but this was because I positioned the ramets in a consistent geometric pattern; it would take much less time with a team of volunteers who need only approximate spacing and densities to reduce intraspecific competition.
[65] (dis) This is a proximate and local-scale solution that addresses immediate threats of exotic species and a lack of native species for ecological restoration.
[66] (dis) Longer-term, if many locales adopt the planting of species like S. canadensis, it may help establish local barriers that mitigate the spread of A. petiolata.
[67] (dis) Ultimately, there may be opportunity to test whether this mitigation occurs and whether there is creation of a possible nurse layer of an understory species.
[68] (dis) If so, a forest edge ecosystem may redevelop one that is less hostile to native species, including the shrubs and trees that will give it a more impermeable structure.
[69] (dis) If S. canadensis ultimately can be demonstrated to encourage regeneration of other native species and create nodes producing emigrants able to colonize other areas, then restoration, like invasion, may self-organize and become passive in that sense.
[70] (dis) One question is whether this self-organization actually will occur.
[71] (dis) A second question is whether S. canadensis or any returning native species will begin to experience densitydependent herbivory or long-term problems related to fragmentation impacts on ant dispersal of its seeds.
[72] (dis) Though it remains to be determined whether the necessary ecosystem functions will return and how much active restoration will be needed, if there are simultaneous larger-scale efforts to conserve interior forest ecosystems and reduce fragmentation, then the rate of active and passive restoration of forest edges eventually will be able to catch up and overtake the rate of damage.
